nameStory: The brown-headed cowbird earned its name from its habit of following grazing cattle and horses, feeding on insects stirred up by their hooves. Originally called the "buffalo bird" when vast herds of bison roamed the plains, these clever birds adapted to farm life as settlers brought livestock eastward. Their chocolate-brown heads give them the second part of their common name.
description: Brown-headed cowbirds are compact songbirds about the size of a robin, with males sporting glossy black bodies and rich brown heads that shine in sunlight. Females are smaller and dressed in streaky gray-brown plumage that helps them blend into their surroundings. These social birds often gather in mixed flocks with other blackbirds, especially during migration and winter. They're famous (or infamous) for being "brood parasites" - they lay their eggs in other birds' nests and let the foster parents do all the work.

idTips.label: Male's contrasting colors
idTips.description: Males have an unmistakable chocolate-brown head that contrasts sharply with their iridescent black body - like they're wearing a brown helmet over a shiny black suit

idTips.label: Female's streaky appearance
idTips.description: Females are smaller and covered in soft gray-brown streaks with a slightly paler throat, resembling a large sparrow but with a thicker, more pointed bill

idTips.label: Body shape and posture
idTips.description: Compact and sturdy with a relatively large head, short tail, and thick neck - they often hold their heads high with a confident, upright posture when walking

idTips.label: Bill characteristics
idTips.description: Dark, thick, pointed bill perfect for cracking seeds and catching insects - noticeably stouter than most sparrows but not as heavy as a grackle's

idTips.label: Flocking behavior
idTips.description: Often seen in mixed groups with red-winged blackbirds and grackles, walking confidently on the ground rather than hopping like many songbirds

habitat: Brown-headed cowbirds thrive in open and semi-open habitats across New England, including farmland, pastures, suburban lawns, and forest edges. They're especially common around livestock operations, horse farms, and areas where cattle graze, but you'll also find them in parks, golf courses, and backyard feeders. They prefer areas that mix open ground for foraging with nearby trees or shrubs for perching and shelter.

seasonality.spring: Males return from southern wintering grounds in March and April, often arriving before females and establishing territories with their distinctive liquid, gurgling songs that sound like water being poured from a bottle.
seasonality.summer: Peak breeding season when you'll see males puffing up their feathers and performing courtship displays, while females secretly search for other birds' nests to lay their eggs in - look for them following other songbirds.
seasonality.fall: Large flocks begin forming in late summer and early fall, often mixing with other blackbird species in agricultural areas and staging areas before migration south.
seasonality.winter: Most individuals migrate south, but some may linger at bird feeders in southern New England during mild winters, especially if food sources remain abundant.

funFact: A single female brown-headed cowbird can lay up to 80 eggs per season in the nests of other bird species, making her one of nature's most prolific moms - and she never builds a nest or raises a single chick herself!
confusionNotes: Female cowbirds are often mistaken for large sparrows or female red-winged blackbirds, but cowbirds have thicker bills, more uniform streaking, and walk rather than hop. Males are sometimes confused with male red-winged blackbirds, but remember: cowbirds have brown heads and black bodies, while red-wings have red shoulder patches and are entirely black elsewhere.
contextualKnowledge: Brown-headed cowbirds were originally plains birds that followed bison herds, but European settlement and forest clearing allowed them to expand eastward into New England. Their brood parasitism has contributed to declines in some forest songbird populations, making them a species that's both fascinating from a natural history perspective and concerning from a conservation standpoint.
compareHints: Brown-headed cowbirds are the only members of their genus in New England, but they're closely related to other blackbirds in the icterid family. Unlike red-winged blackbirds which have distinctive shoulder patches, or common grackles which are much larger with longer tails and iridescent purple-green bodies, cowbirds are more compact with their unique brown-and-black male coloration. They're also the only blackbirds in the region that practice brood parasitism.
